events.title: Arts in Education Week Celebration and Proclamation Reading
events.description:
The Portland Art Museum, in partnership with Portland Public Schools and the Office of Arts & Culture, is celebrating Arts in Education Week, recognized nationally, September 13–19. Please join us on Tuesday, September 15 at 1 p.m. in the Silver Family Youth and Community Gallery at the Portland Art Museum for a City of Portland proclamation reading. 

The gallery hosts the extraordinary work of student artists in the HeART of Portland Visual Art Exhibition. This exhibition features over 100 works that highlight the diversity of arts offerings across Portland Public Schools. As part of the proclamation reading, elementary students will share their artwork.

register here

Admission is free. Registration requested.

Arts in Education Week, September 13–19, is a national celebration that lifts up the enduring power of an arts education. Arts education allows students to develop artistic disciplines, learn about and understand multiple perspectives, build connections with others, and find their voice in the world. Engagement in the arts fosters durable skills such as creativity, problem solving, collaboration, communication, resiliency, and critical thinking. These durable skills will be used by students throughout their lives.  

The arts are not extra; they are an essential part of a well-rounded education. Portland guarantees all 28,000 public elementary students access to an arts education through the Arts Access Fund, powered by the Arts Education Tax. The Arts Access Fund also provides grants for arts organizations that provide arts experiences for K-12 students and people in underserved communities. Last year, local arts organizations recorded a combined 143,525 arts experiences for K-12 students in Portland.   

We are proud to celebrate a 100+ year partnership with Portland Public Schools, and each year the Portland Art Museum serves 30,000 students through school tours and community access programs. Children 17 and under are always free.

events.title: The Maker’s Table | A Winemaker Dinner Series
events.description:
Portland Art Museum Venues invites you to The Maker’s Table—an intimate evening series bringing together Oregon winemakers and visual artists for a one-of-a-kind experience of wine, art and conversation.

Held after hours in the Museum’s stunning new Rothko Pavillion, each evening explores the creative process behind both disciplines. Guests are invited not to simply taste and observe, but to engage; discovering how inspiration takes shape, how tension fuels beauty, and how artistry evolves over time.  

This season of our Maker’s Table Series will include five unforgettable events—each featuring a different visual artist represented by the Portland Art Museum’s Rental Sales Gallery paired with an Oregon winery.

Guests may choose from three experiences: the Tasting Experience (6 – 8 p.m.), the Maker’s Table Dinner (Tasting + Dinner), or for the Collector’s Table Dinner Series, which includes tickets to all five events.

 Tasting Experience (6 – 8 p.m.) | $135

A conversation driven, walk-around tasting in the Rothko Pavillion’s Community Commons featuring curated wine pours, seasonal passed appetizers, and artwork on view throughout the space.  The experience includes a moderated conversation between the featured winemaker and visual artist. 

Seated Winemaker Dinner | $295 

Begin the evening with the Pre-Dinner Tasting followed by a three-course, plated dinner with curated wine pairings, and a chef-driven menu. 

This meal will take place in the Rothko Pavilion’s third floor gallery, overlooking both the city and the museum’s magnificent Grand Gallery.  Guests will be joined by that evening’s featured winemaker and visual artist for a more intimate continuation of the conversation.

The Maker’s Table Season Lineup

  • May 21, 2026 | Alexana Winery – Winemaker Tresider Burns + Visual Artist: Hazel Schlesinger (RSG Artist)
  • June 18, 2026 | Big Table Farm – Winemaker Brian Marcy & Clare Carver + Visual Artist: Clare Carver (of Big Table Farm)
  • July 16, 2026 | Antica Terra – Winemaker Maggie Harrison + Visual Artist Vince Skelly (of Marta Gallery)
  • August 20, 2026 | Cristom Vineyards – Winemaker Daniel Estrin + Visual Artist: Satoko Motouji (RSG Artist) 
  • September 17, 2026 | Soter Vineyards – Winemaker Tony Soter + Visual Artist: Dave Haslett (RSG Artist)

Seating is limited for each event. We encourage early booking.

Proceeds from The Maker’s Table series help the mission of the Portland Art Museum

events.title: Star 80 x Director Fits
events.description:
Star 80 (1983) Directed by Bob Fosse. 1hr 43min. Rated R.

Star 80 is presented by Director Fits as part of a series on Fashion and Film. A disturbing, beautiful, and haunting film about the rise-and-fall of Dorothy Stratten. 

“Four stars! An important movie. Devastating, violent, hopeless, and important, because it holds a mirror up to a part of the world we live in, and helps us see it more clearly.” – Roger Ebert

Director Fits is a media platform focusing on the everyday sartorial decisions of filmmakers. We believe that directors are an often overlooked group of impeccably well-dressed artists making bold choices when it comes to clothing. We focus on their personal style, the practical garments they wear while they work, their buttoned-up red carpet looks, and so much more. We dive deep into the thought process of a director’s view on clothing and how it affects them as well as their films.

We do not generally provide advisories about subject matter or potentially triggering content in films, and films exhibited don’t necessarily reflect the views of PAM CUT or the Portland Art Museum. In addition to the synopses, trailers, and other links on our website, further information about content and age-appropriateness for specific films can be found on sites like Common Sense Media, IMDb, and DoesTheDogDie.com.

events.title: Art in ASL + Look With Me
events.description:
Portland Art Museum celebrates the Deaf Community with Art in ASL on the 3rd Sunday of every month. Deaf Community members and their companions enjoy complimentary admission all day and are invited to participate in guided Look with Me sessions in the galleries between 12-3pm. Visitors of all ages are welcome.

Some Look with Me sessions will be led in ASL and some will be led in English. All sessions will have interpretation. Look for signs in the galleries to find locations of each session.

Join us for slow looking sessions from 12-3 pm then come to the Finley Studio for artmaking and social time from 3-5 pm.

Look With Me does not require special tickets. Museum tickets can be purchased online or at the box office.

Accessibility:
The museum galleries are wheelchair, mobility device, and stroller accessible. Complimentary stools, folding chairs, manual wheelchairs, and assistive technology are available upon request. All museum accessibility info is available here. Please contact us with any additional access needs at access@pam.org or leave a videophone message at 503-420-3169.

Art in ASL is presented in partnership with the Deaf Look Club, a program of Bridge City Montessori.

events.title: Kika x Director Fits
events.description:
Kika (1993) Directed by Pedro Almodóvar. 1hr 54min. Not Rated.

Kika is presented by Director Fits as part of a series on Fashion and Film. Kika is a black comedy by Pedro Almodóvar that follows a young makeup artist sent to prepare a corpse when her attentions bring him back to life. Featuring a Jean Paul Gaultier wardrobe, this stylish film helped cement the “Almodóvar look.”

“Kika marked the first collaboration between the French designer and the Spanish filmmaker. Gaultier was responsible for the costumes of Abril’s character, Andrea Caracortada, who played a sadistic television presenter with a love for gore” – Director Fits

events.title: Siren: The Voices of Shelley Beattie w/ Irene Taylor Q&A
events.description:
Siren: The Voices of Shelley Beattie (2026).
Directed by Irene Taylor. 1hr 43min.
Courtesy of HBO Documentary Films

This film will be shown with open captions, and the Q&A will have ASL interpretation. Audio Description available.

Join us for the Portland Premiere of Irene Taylor‘s latest film, Siren: The Voices of Shelley Beattie. Following the screening, Irene Taylor will join us for a moderated Q&A. 

While searching the internet one day, Hollywood veteran Marlee Matlin came upon the story of athlete Shelley Beattie – a fellow deaf woman whose life felt eerily like her own. Both women had experienced adventure and fame, but also discrimination, abuse, and addiction while navigating a hearing world. SIREN: THE VOICES OF SHELLEY BEATTIE explores the parallels between the two legendary women in a haunting portrait of strength, beauty, and resiliency. 

Guided by Academy Award® winner Matlin, the film utilizes a wealth of archival footage, home video, intimate interviews, and Beattie’s striking personal artwork to convey her vibrant personality and voice. Matlin sought out acclaimed documentary filmmaker Irene Taylor who has been exploring themes of hearing loss and family in many of her award-winning films for decades.  Together Taylor and Matlin decided to excavate Shelly’s extraordinary story. By bringing Beattie’s story to light, Matlin and Taylor illuminate how the hearing world can be an isolating and cruel place for those who are deaf. Beattie found safety by protecting herself with a strong, physical exterior, then became a top international bodybuilder in the 1990s, and starred as the character “Siren” on TV’s hugely popular “American Gladiators”. But beneath her tough armor was a troubled and sensitive spirit. The film traces Beattie’s early challenges with deafness in a family that struggled to understand her, detailing her journey to breaking barriers in sports and media, and highlighting her advocacy for mental health awareness all before her death at 40 years old. Matlin’s quest to learn about Beattie is an exploration into what it takes to overcome inner demons and personal struggles, while turning deafness into a strength to transcend limitations and shatter boundaries.

events.title: The Stars We Do Not See: Opening Conversation
events.description:
Join us in celebrating the landmark exhibition The Stars We Do Not See: Australian Indigenous Art. In conversation, our distinguished guests explore the rich history, contemporary narratives, and power of Indigenous art.

Moderated by Kathleen Ash-Milby, Curator of Native American Art at the Portland Art Museum, the discussion will feature Dr. Jessica Clark, Senior Curator of First Nations Art at the National Gallery of Victoria (NGV), alongside renowned artist and documentary photographer Ricky Maynard. Together, they will broadly reflect on the living cultural traditions, artistic innovations, and socio-political themes represented in the exhibition with a specific focus on Ricky Maynard’s work.

Featured Speakers

  • Dr. Jessica Clark is a proud Trawlwoolway woman and a curator with a background in art history and education, born in Lutruwita/Trowunna and currently living and working on Wurundjeri Country in Naarm/Melbourne. Clark currently holds the position of Senior Curator, First Nations Art at the National Gallery of Victoria. Previous institution- based curatorial positions include: Curator at the Australian Centre for Contemporary Art (ACCA) (2022–25); Curatorial Manager, Victorian First Peoples Art and Design Fair at Creative Victoria (2024–25); and Ursula Hoff Fellow, University of Melbourne (2024–26). Clark holds a PhD Fine Art and Music (2023), Victorian College of the Arts, University of Melbourne, of which was awarded The Chancellor’s Prize for Excellence 2024.
  • Ricky Maynard (Ben Lomond and Cape Portland) is a Tasmanian documentary photographer, activist, and social commentator whose work is featured in The Stars We Do Not See. He is celebrated internationally for his powerful documentary series, including his groundbreaking portraits of Wik elders—the traditional custodians of Cape York Peninsula in Far North Queensland.
  • Kathleen Ash-Milby, a member of the Navajo Nation, and Senior Curator of Native American Art, has worked at the Museum since 2019, expanding engagement with Indigenous artists through major acquisitions and exhibitions. Prior to joining PAM, she spent 19 years at the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, organizing numerous solo and thematic exhibitions across a wide range of media. She is an accomplished scholar, published author, and former president of the Native American Art Studies Association.

events.title: Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World
events.description:
Mary Oliver: Saved by the Beauty of the World (2026) Directed by Sasha Waters Freyer. 1hr 31min. Not Rated.

If poetry had a pop icon, Mary Oliver would be it. Best-selling poet and Pulitzer Prize-winner, lover of dogs and long walks in the woods, queer and out but intensely private—Oliver’s poems inspire liberals and conservatives, atheists and believers, naturalists and urbanites. She was America’s unlikely, contemporary mystic, stalking the ponds and forests of Cape Cod for nearly fifty years in order to open herself—and us, her readers—to the known and unknowable world. Sasha Waters’ beguiling portrait features poems read by Helena Bonham Carter, Steve Buscemi, Stephen Colbert, Lucy Dacus, Jesse Welles, and Oprah Winfrey.

events.title: Evening for Educators: The Stars We Do Not See: Australian Indigenous Art
events.description:
Overview

This significant exhibition introduces North American audiences to the diverse and distinct visual iconographies of Indigenous Australia, which is made up of more than 250 distinct Indigenous nations. Explore this rich and living history of creativity through over 200 works made by more than 130 artists. Drawn exclusively from the collection of Melbourne’s National Gallery of Victoria, The Stars We Do Not See offers a rare opportunity to experience important watershed moments of modern and contemporary Australian Indigenous art. 

Join us for an evening of learning and conversation with special guests:

  • Dr. Jessica Clark is a proud Trawlwoolway woman and a curator with a background in art history and education, born in Lutruwita/Trowunna and currently living and working on Wurundjeri Country in Naarm/Melbourne. Clark currently holds the position of Senior Curator, First Nations Art at the National Gallery of Victoria. Previous institution- based curatorial positions include: Curator at the Australian Centre for Contemporary Art (ACCA) (2022–25); Curatorial Manager, Victorian First Peoples Art and Design Fair at Creative Victoria (2024–25); and Ursula Hoff Fellow, University of Melbourne (2024–26). Clark holds a PhD Fine Art and Music (2023), Victorian College of the Arts, University of Melbourne, of which was awarded The Chancellor’s Prize for Excellence 2024.
  • Ricky Maynard (Pakana) is a Tasmanian documentary photographer, activist, and social commentator whose work is featured in The Stars We Do Not See. He is celebrated internationally for his powerful documentary series, including his groundbreaking portraits of Wik elders—the traditional custodians of Cape York Peninsula in Far North Queensland.

Come away with resources to connect your students with this powerful exhibition.

Program schedule

  • 5:15–6:00 p.m. | Pre-Program Exhibition Viewing + Refreshments
    The Stars We Do Not See and the Commons, Main Museum
    Enjoy self-guided time and slow-looking conversations in the exhibition with PAM Learning staff. Light refreshments available in the Museum Commons.
  • 6:00–7:00 p.m. | Presentation + Discussion
    Whitsell Auditorium, Main Museum, Lower Level
    Presentation and discussion with Kathleen Ash-Milby, Portland Art Museum Senior Curator of Native American Art; Dr. Jessica Clark, Senior Curator, First Nations Art at the National Gallery of Victoria; and photographer Ricky Maynard.
  • 7:00 – 7:30 p.m. | Exhibition Viewing + Educator Resources
    The Stars We Do Not See and Whitsell Auditorium, Main Museum
    Discuss educator resources and spend additional time in the exhibition.

events.title: Free First Thursday: Stars We Do Not See
events.description:
Overview

Join us during October’s Free First Thursday for a special free film program presented in conjunction with The Stars We Do Not See: Australian Indigenous Art. The screenings celebrate film and video work by and about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island people, offering another way to explore the stories, histories, and perspectives at the heart of The Stars We Do Not See.

Film schedule

2 p.m.  BeDevil (1993)
Directed by Tracey Moffatt | Runtime: 90 mins

The first feature film directed by an Australian Aboriginal woman, Tracey Moffat’s debut feature BeDevil was inspired by ghost stories she heard as a child from her extended Aboriginal and Irish Australian family. Moffatt constructs a trilogy in which characters are haunted by the past and bewitched by memories, with all three stories set in her highly stylized, hyper-real, and hyper-imaginary Australian landscape. In the first story Mister Chuck, a young boy is fascinated and terrified by a swamp that is haunted by the ghost of an American GI. Choo Choo Choo Choo finds a family living by railroad tracks haunted by strange happenings. The mother, played by Moffatt, is drawn to the tracks at night as she senses the horror of a past tragedy. The final story, Lovin’ the Spin I’m In, follows a woman who resists eviction attempts by her landlord so she can keep vigil for her dead son. (NGV)

5 p.m. The Drover’s Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson (2021)
Directed by Leah Purcell | Runtime: 109 mins

Written by, directed by, and starring Leah Purcell (Goa-Gunggari-Wakka Wakka), this searing revisionist Western reimagines a classic piece of colonial literature. In 1893 on an isolated property, a heavily pregnant woman named Molly Johnson (Leah Purcell) and her children struggle to survive the harsh Australian landscape; her husband is gone, droving sheep in the high country. Molly then finds herself confronted by a shackled Aboriginal fugitive named Yadaka (Rob Collins). As an unlikely bond begins to form between them, secrets unravel about her true identity. Meanwhile, realizing Molly’s husband is missing, new town lawman Nate Clintoff becomes suspicious and sends his constable to investigate. The deadly encounter between Molly, Yadaka and the constable results in a tragic chain of events with Molly becoming a symbol of feminism and anti-racism. (Rotten Tomatoes)

Free admission all day. Come see The Stars We Do Not See, experience the films, and spend a day exploring the art and stories of Indigenous Australia.

events.title: Capturing Bigfoot // Presented by the Oregon Historical Society
events.description:
On October 20, 1967, Roger Patterson captured 59 seconds of film showing a creature walking through the Northern California woods—footage that became the most analyzed and debated in history. Fifty-nine years later, a reel of 16mm film discovered in a safe changes everything. 

“Capturing Bigfoot” reveals the untold story behind the world’s greatest mystery, told for the first time by Patterson’s own son and the people who were there. 

This is a story about family legacy, broken friendships, and belief itself. 

Q&A participants:  Marq Evans (Director), Tamir Ardon (Producer), Clint Patterson (Son of Roger Patterson who shot the original 1967 PG Bigfoot film)

This is a special event screening pre-film general release, which is scheduled for October 20th. Due to the sensitive nature of the never-before-seen footage in the film, all recording devices such as phones, meta glasses, etc. will be prohibited in the theater during the film’s showing. We appreciate your cooperation.

events.title: Eraserhead (1977) x Fresh Cut Flowers
events.description:
Eraserhead (1977) Directed by David Lynch. 1hr 29min. Not Rated.

Fresh Cut Flowers and PAM CUT have partnered to present “Night Blooming Jasmine,” a weekend-long special screening of David Lynch films this Fall. Celebrating the intersection of nature, beauty, mystery, and the surreal – Lynch’s distinctive visual language and ability to find the strange within the everyday closely align with the sensibility Fresh Cut Flowers brings to its work. Opening with Eraserhead (1977). Eraserhead is not only a surreal horror cult classic, but Lynch’s first feature film. The film explores fatherhood, anxiety, and alienation against a dystopian and noisy backdrop of dream logic. 

Along with the screening, Fresh Cut Flowers will release a small collection of Night Blooming Jasmine products.

FRESH CUT FLOWERS is a contemporary lifestyle brand and floral studio based out of Portland, OR. Trey Hales (Founder, Designer) and Cody Shulund (Floral Director) deliver compelling nature-focused storytelling through thoughtfully designed products & well-executed floral work to paint a vivid picture of the world the brand builds. 

The brand operates a store inside Machus (1101 SW Alder St), featuring rotating drops of clothing alongside a selection of classic, core pieces. The brand’s floral studio produces more than 25 events each year across Portland, New York, and Los Angeles, creating floral experiences for weddings, parties, installations, and other events that bring the brand’s distinctive point of view to life.
